decks.title: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties — Part 1: the table, blocks, names and sizes
goals: Explain Mendeleev’s periodic law, its merits and defects, and the modern periodic law
Locate an element in the long form of the table from its configuration and write IUPAC names for Z > 100
Explain the trends in atomic and ionic radii using nuclear charge and shielding

slides.heading: Organising the elements
slides.body_md: Part 1: why elements are classified, how Mendeleev and Moseley arranged them, the long form of the table and the trends in size.

slides.narration: Welcome. More than a hundred elements are known, and learning each one separately would be impossible. In this part we see how classification began with Mendeleev, how the modern table is arranged by atomic number, how new elements are named, and why atoms get smaller across a period and larger down a group.

slides.heading: The need for classification; Mendeleev’s law
slides.body_md: Grouping elements with similar properties lets us **study many elements through a few patterns** and **predict** the properties of new ones. **Mendeleev (1869)**: the properties of elements are a **periodic function of their atomic masses**. He placed elements in rows (periods) and columns (groups) so that similar elements fell together.

rows: Too many elements to study singly
Learn the pattern of each group instead
Gaps in the table point to them
Position gives valency and type of oxide

visual.alt: Table of the needs met by classifying elements and how a periodic table helps

slides.narration: Classifying elements lets us learn patterns rather than facts one at a time, and lets us predict the behaviour of elements we have not yet studied. Mendeleev proposed that the properties of elements repeat periodically when they are arranged by atomic mass. He arranged them in rows and columns so that elements with similar properties came together.

slides.heading: Merits of Mendeleev’s table
slides.body_md: Mendeleev **left gaps** rather than force elements into the wrong group, and **predicted** the properties of three missing elements, later found: **gallium** (eka-aluminium), **scandium** (eka-boron) and **germanium** (eka-silicon). He also **corrected doubtful atomic masses**, and the **noble gases** later fitted in as a new group without upsetting the table.

visual.alt: Table comparing Mendeleev’s predicted atomic masses and oxide formulae with the elements discovered later

slides.narration: The great strength of Mendeleev’s table was that it left gaps for elements not yet discovered and described their properties in advance. Gallium, scandium and germanium, found later, matched his predictions closely in atomic mass and in the formulae of their oxides. He also corrected some doubtful atomic masses, and the noble gases fitted in later as a new group.

slides.heading: Defects of the table; the modern periodic law
slides.body_md: Defects: **hydrogen** has no fixed place; some elements are out of order of atomic mass (**Ar, K; Co, Ni; Te, I**); **isotopes** have no places of their own; unlike elements share a group; lanthanoids and actinoids have no proper place. **Moseley (1913)**: the **modern periodic law** says properties are a periodic function of **atomic number**.

headers: How the modern law removes it
rows: Ar before K, Co before Ni, Te before I by mass
Atomic number gives the order Ar, K; Co, Ni; Te, I
Isotopes share one atomic number, so one place
Atomic number: periodicity follows electronic configuration

slides.narration: Mendeleev’s table had defects. Hydrogen had no fixed place, a few elements were out of order of atomic mass, and isotopes had no places of their own. Moseley showed that the atomic number, not the mass, is the true basis. The modern periodic law says the properties of elements are a periodic function of atomic number, and this removes those defects.

slides.body_md: Decide what the discovery of gallium showed about Mendeleev’s law.
slides.narration: Quick check. Mendeleev gave an atomic mass and an oxide formula for an element that nobody had found. When gallium was discovered it matched. Think about what this agreement proves about the usefulness of a periodic law, and what it does not prove about the basis of the arrangement, then choose the statement that fits best.

slides.heading: The long form of the periodic table
slides.body_md: The table has **7 periods** (rows) and **18 groups** (columns). Elements are placed by **atomic number**, so an element’s **period** is its outermost shell and its **group** follows from the valence configuration. The **s, p, d and f blocks** have **14, 36, 40 and 28** elements.

The metalloids sit along the staircase between metals and non-metals. The two f-block rows are drawn below the main table so that it does not become too wide.

slides.heading: Blocks, groups and IUPAC numbering
slides.body_md: The **block** is the subshell that receives the last electron. **s block**: groups 1, 2 (and He); **p block**: groups 13 to 18, group number $= 12 +$ outer electrons; **d block**: groups 3 to 12, group number $=$ $(n-1)d$ plus $ns$ electrons; **f block**: lanthanoids and actinoids. IUPAC numbers the groups **1 to 18**; the old labels IA–VIIA, VIII and 0 are also accepted.

visual.alt: Table of the four blocks with valence configurations, IUPAC group numbers and older labels

slides.narration: The block of an element is the type of subshell that receives its last electron. The s block is groups one and two, the p block is groups thirteen to eighteen, the d block is groups three to twelve, and the f block is placed below. IUPAC numbers the groups one to eighteen, and the older labels with Roman numerals are still accepted.

slides.heading: Worked example: position from the configuration
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Locate (a) the element with configuration $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^7\,4s^2$ and (b) the element of atomic number 52.

**(a)** Last electron in $3d$: **d block**. Period = highest $n$ = 4. Group = $7 + 2 = 9$. Atomic number $= 18 + 9 = 27$, Co: block d, period 4, group 9.

**(b)** $Z = 52$: [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s² 5p⁴. Last electron in $5p$: **p block**; period 5; group $= 12 + 4 = 16$. The element is Te.

visual.alt: Table of the configuration, block, period and group of cobalt and tellurium

slides.narration: For the first element the last electron enters three d, so it is in the d block. The highest shell is the fourth, so it is in period four. Seven plus two valence electrons make group nine, which is cobalt. For atomic number fifty two, the last electron enters five p, so it is in the p block, period five and group sixteen, which is tellurium.

slides.heading: IUPAC names for elements with Z above 100
slides.body_md: Until a name is approved, an element gets a **temporary systematic name** built from **numerical roots for each digit** of its atomic number, ending in **-ium**; the symbol is the **first letters** of the roots. Roots: **0 nil, 1 un, 2 bi, 3 tri, 4 quad, 5 pent, 6 hex, 7 sept, 8 oct, 9 enn**.

visual.alt: Table of the numerical roots and their symbol letters for the digits zero to nine

slides.narration: Elements above atomic number one hundred receive a temporary name until a permanent one is approved. Each digit of the atomic number is replaced by a root: nil for zero, un for one, bi for two, tri, quad, pent, hex, sept, oct and enn for the rest. The roots are joined and the ending ium is added. The symbol uses the first letter of each root.

slides.heading: Worked example: names from atomic numbers
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Write the temporary IUPAC names and symbols for $Z = 114$ and $Z = 120$, and find $Z$ for *ununseptium*.

**114:** 1, 1, 4 → un, un, quad → **ununquadium**, symbol **Uuq**.

**120:** 1, 2, 0 → un, bi, nil → **unbinilium**, symbol **Ubn**.

**ununseptium:** un, un, sept → 1, 1, 7 → $Z = 117$.

visual.alt: Table of three atomic numbers with their roots, temporary names and symbols

slides.narration: Take one hundred fourteen. The digits one, one and four give the roots un, un and quad, so the name is ununquadium and the symbol is capital U, small u, small q. For one hundred twenty the roots are un, bi and nil, giving unbinilium. Going backwards, ununseptium has roots un, un and sept, which is one, one and seven, so the atomic number is one hundred seventeen.

slides.heading: Atomic radius and its trends
slides.body_md: Atomic radius is **half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms**: **covalent radius** for non-metals, **metallic radius** for metals. **Across a period** it **decreases**; **down a group** it **increases**.

slides.narration: The atomic radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. It is called the covalent radius for non-metals and the metallic radius for metals. Across a period the radius falls steadily, from sodium to chlorine. Down a group it rises, because each new period adds an extra shell, as the group one bars show.

slides.heading: Nuclear charge, shielding and valence electrons
slides.body_md: Across a period the **nuclear charge rises** while electrons enter the **same shell**, so **shielding hardly changes** and the **effective nuclear charge** grows: the **valence electrons** (their number rises from 1 to 7 across period 3) are pulled in. Down a group the **number of valence electrons stays the same**, but extra shells add **shielding** and distance.

slides.narration: Two factors control size: nuclear charge and shielding. Across a period each atom has one more proton and one more valence electron in the same shell. The inner electrons shield equally, so the pull on the valence electrons grows and the atom shrinks. Down a group the valence electron number stays the same, but extra shells add shielding and distance.

slides.body_md: A **cation** is **smaller** than its atom: electrons are lost, often a whole shell, and the **same nuclear charge** pulls the rest in. An **anion** is **larger**: the extra electron raises **electron–electron repulsion** while the nuclear charge is unchanged. More positive charge gives a smaller cation (Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺).

slides.narration: These six ions all have ten electrons, so they are isoelectronic. What differs is the number of protons. Nitride has seven and is the largest. Aluminium has thirteen and its three plus ion is the smallest. With the same electron cloud, more protons pull it in more strongly, so the radius falls as the atomic number rises.

slides.heading: Worked example: ordering ionic radii
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Arrange $\ce{Mg^2+}$, $\ce{Na+}$, $\ce{F-}$ and $\ce{O^2-}$ in increasing order of radius and explain.

All four have **10 electrons**. Nuclear charges: Mg 12, Na 11, F 9, O 8. The more protons, the stronger the pull, so the radius **decreases with increasing $Z$**.

Increasing radius: Mg²⁺ < Na⁺ < F⁻ < O²⁻ (72, 102, 133, 140 pm).

visual.alt: Table of the nuclear charge, electrons and radius of Mg2+, Na+, F− and O2−

slides.narration: All four ions have ten electrons, so the only difference is the nuclear charge. Magnesium has twelve protons and holds its electrons most tightly, so its ion is the smallest. Then come sodium, fluoride and oxide, which has the fewest protons and the largest radius. So the order of increasing radius is magnesium, sodium, fluoride, oxide.

slides.narration: Welcome to Part Two. Here we move from sizes to energies: how much energy it takes to remove an electron, how much is released when one is added, and how strongly an atom attracts bonding electrons. We then use these ideas to explain valence, the odd behaviour of second period elements, diagonal pairs and the nature of oxides.

slides.heading: Ionisation enthalpy and what controls it
slides.body_md: The **first ionisation enthalpy** is the energy needed to remove the most loosely held electron from **one mole of gaseous atoms**: $\text{X(g)} \to \text{X}^+\text{(g)} + e^-$, in **kJ mol⁻¹**; it is always positive. It **increases** with **nuclear charge**, **decreases** with **atomic size** and **shielding**, and is higher for **filled or half-filled** subshells.

slides.narration: Ionisation enthalpy is the energy needed to remove the most loosely held electron from a mole of gaseous atoms. It is always positive. It rises with nuclear charge and falls with larger size and more shielding. An electron in an s orbital is held more strongly than one in a p orbital of the same shell, and filled or half filled subshells add stability.

slides.heading: The pattern and its irregularities
slides.body_md: In general it **rises across a period** and **falls down a group**. slides.heading: Worked example: successive ionisation enthalpies
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The first three ionisation enthalpies of an element are 520, 7298, 11815 kJ mol⁻¹ (lithium). Find the number of valence electrons and the group.

Ratios of successive values: 14.0 and 1.6. The **huge jump** (about 14.0 times) comes after the **1st** removal: the second electron comes from the **stable inner shell** ($1s^2$).

So there is **1 valence electron**: group **1**.

visual.alt: Table of the first three ionisation enthalpies of lithium with the ratio of each to the previous value

slides.narration: Look at the ratios of successive values. The second ionisation enthalpy is about fourteen times the first, a huge jump, while the third is only a little larger than the second. The big jump shows that the second electron must come from a stable inner shell. So the element has just one valence electron and belongs to group one.

slides.body_md: The **electron gain enthalpy** is the enthalpy change when **one mole of gaseous atoms each gain an electron**: $\text{X(g)} + e^- \to \text{X}^-\text{(g)}$. It is **negative** when energy is released (halogens most negative). **Cl is more negative than F**: in the small F atom the added electron feels strong repulsion from the crowded 2p electrons. **Noble gases are positive**; the second electron gain enthalpy is always positive.

Noble gases have positive values, since the added electron would go into a new shell.

slides.heading: Electronegativity
slides.body_md: **Electronegativity** is the **tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared electron pair** towards itself. It has **no unit** (Pauling scale: F = 4.0, the highest). It **increases across a period** and **decreases down a group**. The **difference** in electronegativity decides **bond polarity**: the larger the difference, the more ionic the bond.

visual.alt: Table of Pauling electronegativity values for selected elements

slides.narration: Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared electron pair towards itself. It has no unit. On the Pauling scale fluorine is highest at four. It rises across a period and falls down a group. The difference between the values for two bonded atoms tells us how polar the bond is, and a large difference means an ionic bond.

slides.heading: Worked example: bond polarity from electronegativity
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Using Pauling values Na 0.9, H 2.1, C 2.5 and Cl 3.0, arrange the bonds Na–Cl, H–Cl, C–Cl and Cl–Cl in order of decreasing polarity.

$\Delta\text{EN}$: Na–Cl $= 3.0 - 0.9 = 2.1$; H–Cl $= 3.0 - 2.1 = 0.9$; C–Cl $= 3.0 - 2.5 = 0.5$; Cl–Cl $= 0.0$.

Order: Na–Cl (ionic) > H–Cl > C–Cl > Cl–Cl (non-polar).

visual.alt: Table of electronegativity differences and bond character for four bonds

slides.narration: Subtract the electronegativities for each bond. Sodium and chlorine differ by two point one, which is so large that the bond is ionic. Hydrogen and chlorine differ by zero point nine and the bond is polar covalent. Carbon and chlorine differ by only zero point five. Two chlorine atoms have no difference, so the bond is non polar.

slides.heading: Metallic and non-metallic character
slides.body_md: **Metallic character** is the tendency to **lose electrons** to form cations; it follows **low ionisation enthalpy and low electronegativity**. It **decreases across a period** and **increases down a group**; non-metallic character does the opposite. **Metalloids** (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) lie on the dividing staircase.

visual.alt: Table of metallic and non-metallic character by position with ionisation enthalpy and electronegativity

slides.narration: Metallic character is the tendency to lose electrons and form cations. It goes with a low ionisation enthalpy and a low electronegativity. It falls across a period and rises down a group. In group fourteen, carbon is a non metal, silicon and germanium are metalloids, and tin and lead are metals. Non metallic character follows the opposite trend.

slides.heading: Valence and oxidation states
slides.body_md: The **valency** of a main-group element is set by its **valence electrons**: toward **oxygen** it equals the group number (1 to 7); toward **hydrogen** it rises to 4 and then falls ($8 -$ group). The **oxidation state** is the charge an atom would have if all bonds were ionic. **d-block** elements show **several** oxidation states because $ns$ and $(n-1)d$ electrons have similar energies.

visual.alt: Table of the group, hydride, valency toward hydrogen, highest oxide and oxidation state for the elements of period 3

slides.narration: Valency shows a periodic pattern. Towards oxygen it rises from one to seven across period three, matching the group number. Towards hydrogen it rises to four at silicon and then falls to one at chlorine. Oxidation state is the charge an atom would have if all its bonds were ionic. Transition elements show several oxidation states.

slides.heading: Anomalous behaviour of second-period elements
slides.body_md: Li to F differ from the rest of their groups because of **small size**, **high electronegativity and ionisation enthalpy**, and **no d orbitals**, so the **maximum covalence is 4**. Nitrogen forms NCl₃ but not NCl₅ (phosphorus forms both). Only they form strong **pπ–pπ multiple bonds**: C=C, N≡N, O=O.

rows: No d orbitals in N; covalence limited to 4
B: BF₄⁻ at most four bonds
Small atoms overlap p orbitals sideways
F: lower electron gain enthalpy than Cl

visual.alt: Table of four ways in which a second-period element differs from the next member of its group

slides.narration: The first element of each group in the second period behaves differently from the rest of its group. The reasons are small size, high electronegativity and ionisation enthalpy, and the absence of d orbitals, which limits covalence to four. Nitrogen forms nitrogen trichloride but not the pentachloride, whereas phosphorus forms both. Small atoms also form strong multiple bonds.

slides.heading: Diagonal relationship
slides.body_md: Some elements of period 2 resemble the element **diagonally below and to the right** in period 3: **Li–Mg**, **Be–Al**, **B–Si**. The pairs have similar **electronegativity, charge-to-size ratio and polarising power**. Li and Mg both form nitrides directly and have carbonates that decompose on heating; Be and Al both have amphoteric oxides.

**Problem.** Show with balanced equations that $\ce{Al2O3}$ is amphoteric, and give the equation for the reaction of $\ce{P4O10}$ with water.

Acidic oxide: $\ce{P4O10 + 6H2O -> 4H3PO4}$

notes.title: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Need for classification; Mendeleev’s periodic law, merits and defects
sections.body_md:
Classifying the elements lets us study their properties through patterns and predict the behaviour of elements not yet studied. **Mendeleev's periodic law (1869):** the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their **atomic masses**.

**Merits:** similar elements fell in one group; **gaps** were left for undiscovered elements, whose properties he predicted (eka-aluminium, atomic mass about 68, found as **gallium**, 69.7; eka-silicon, about 72, found as **germanium**, 72.6; eka-boron, about 44, found as **scandium**, 45); some doubtful atomic masses were corrected; the **noble gases** later fitted in as a new group.

**Defects:** hydrogen has no fixed position; some elements are out of order of atomic mass (Ar and K, Co and Ni, Te and I); isotopes have no separate places; unlike elements are grouped together; lanthanoids and actinoids have no proper place.

**Modern periodic law (Moseley, 1913):** the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their **atomic numbers**. It removes these defects: the order is by atomic number, isotopes share one place, and periodicity arises from the periodic recurrence of similar outer electronic configurations.

key_terms.definition_md: The properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses.
The properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.
An element whose existence Mendeleev predicted, named “eka” (one beyond) the element above it.

sections.heading: 2. Long form of the periodic table: periods, groups and blocks
sections.body_md:
The long form has **7 periods** and **18 groups**. The **period number** is the highest principal quantum number n of the element; period lengths are 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32. **IUPAC** numbers the groups 1 to 18 (the old IA–VIIA, VIII and 0 are also accepted).

The **block** is the subshell that receives the last electron. **s block:** groups 1 and 2 (and He); group = number of valence electrons. **p block:** groups 13 to 18; group = 12 + number of outer p electrons (ns² np¹ to ns² np⁶). **d block:** groups 3 to 12; group = number of (n − 1)d plus ns electrons. **f block:** the 14 lanthanoids and 14 actinoids, placed below the table. Together the blocks hold 14 + 36 + 40 + 28 = 118 elements. Metals lie to the left, non-metals to the right, and the **metalloids** (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) along the dividing staircase.

key_terms.definition_md: A horizontal row of the table; its number is the highest shell occupied.
A vertical column of the table (1 to 18); members have similar valence configurations.
The set of elements whose last electron enters the same type of subshell (s, p, d or f).

sections.heading: 3. IUPAC names for elements with Z > 100
sections.body_md:
A new element receives a **temporary systematic name** until the permanent name is approved. Each digit of the atomic number is replaced by a numerical root: **0 nil, 1 un, 2 bi, 3 tri, 4 quad, 5 pent, 6 hex, 7 sept, 8 oct, 9 enn**. The roots are written in order and the ending **-ium** is added; the three-letter symbol uses the first letter of each root (the first letter in capital).

Examples: Z = 114 is un-un-quad, **ununquadium (Uuq)**; Z = 120 is un-bi-nil, **unbinilium (Ubn)**; Z = 117 is un-un-sept, **ununseptium (Uus)**; Z = 101 is un-nil-un, **unnilunium (Unu)**.

key_terms.definition_md: A temporary name built from numerical roots for each digit of the atomic number, ending in -ium.

sections.heading: 4. Atomic and ionic radii; nuclear charge, shielding and valence electrons
sections.body_md:
**Atomic radius** is half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms of the same element: the **covalent radius** for non-metals and the **metallic radius** for metals. **Across a period** the radius **decreases** (Na 186 pm to Cl 99 pm): the nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell, so the shielding by inner electrons hardly changes and the **effective nuclear charge** grows. **Down a group** it **increases** (Li 152 pm to Cs 262 pm): extra shells add distance and shielding.

**Valence electrons** increase by one from group to group across a period and are the **same in number** down a group, which is why members of a group are chemically similar.

A **cation is smaller** than its atom (Na 186 pm, Na⁺ 102 pm); an **anion is larger** (Cl 99 pm, Cl⁻ 181 pm). For **isoelectronic species** the radius falls as the nuclear charge rises: N³⁻ 171 > O²⁻ 140 > F⁻ 133 > Na⁺ 102 > Mg²⁺ 72 > Al³⁺ 54 pm.

key_terms.definition_md: The reduction of the pull of the nucleus on an outer electron by the inner electrons.
The net positive charge felt by a valence electron after shielding.
Atoms or ions with the same number of electrons.

sections.heading: 5. Ionisation enthalpy, electron gain enthalpy, electronegativity and metallic character
sections.body_md:
**Ionisation enthalpy:** energy to remove the outermost electron from one mole of gaseous atoms (kJ mol⁻¹, always positive). It rises with nuclear charge and falls with size and shielding. **Across a period** it rises (with dips: B < Be 801 < 899, Al < Mg 577 < 737, O < N 1314 < 1402, S < P 999 < 1012); **down a group** it falls (Li 520, Na 496, K 419). A very large jump in successive values marks the removal from an inner shell and gives the number of valence electrons.

**Electron gain enthalpy:** enthalpy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron; negative when energy is released. Halogens are most negative; **Cl (-349) is more negative than F (-328)** because of repulsion in the compact 2p shell of F; noble gases are positive.

**Electronegativity:** tendency of a bonded atom to attract the shared electron pair (Pauling scale, no unit; F = 4). It rises across a period and falls down a group. **Metallic character** (tendency to lose electrons) falls across a period and rises down a group; non-metallic character is the reverse.

The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms each gain an electron, X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g).
The tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared pair of electrons.

sections.heading: 6. Valence and oxidation states; second-period anomalies; diagonal relationship
sections.body_md:
The **valency** of a main-group element toward oxygen equals its group number (1 to 7); toward hydrogen it rises to 4 (group 14) and falls to 1 (group 17). The **oxidation state** is the charge an atom would have if all its bonds were ionic; transition elements show several because ns and (n − 1)d electrons have similar energies.

**Second-period anomalies:** Li to F differ from the other members of their groups because of small size, high electronegativity and ionisation enthalpy, and the absence of d orbitals (maximum covalence 4). Nitrogen forms NCl₃ but not NCl₅, whereas phosphorus forms both; only the second-period elements form strong pπ–pπ multiple bonds (C=C, N≡N, O=O).

**Diagonal relationship:** Li–Mg, Be–Al and B–Si resemble each other (similar electronegativity and charge-to-size ratio). Li and Mg form nitrides directly and their carbonates decompose on heating; Be and Al have amphoteric oxides and covalent chlorides; B and Si form acidic oxides and volatile hydrides.

sections.heading: 7. Acidic, basic and amphoteric oxides
sections.body_md:
Across period 3 the oxides change from basic to acidic as the bond to oxygen changes from ionic to covalent: Na₂O strongly basic, MgO basic, **Al₂O₃ amphoteric**, SiO₂ weakly acidic, P₄O₁₀ acidic, SO₃ strongly acidic, Cl₂O₇ very strongly acidic. Basic oxides react with acids, acidic oxides with bases and water, and an amphoteric oxide with both. Down a group the oxides become more basic.

$\ce{Na2O + H2O -> 2NaOH}$; $\ce{Al2O3 + 6HCl -> 2AlCl3 + 3H2O}$ and $\ce{Al2O3 + 2NaOH -> 2NaAlO2 + H2O}$ (amphoteric); $\ce{P4O10 + 6H2O -> 4H3PO4}$; $\ce{SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4}$.

key_terms.definition_md: An oxide that reacts with both acids and bases, such as Al₂O₃.
An oxide that reacts with bases, or with water to give an acid.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Basing the modern law on atomic mass, or Mendeleev's law on atomic number.
- Finding the group of a d-block element from the 4s electrons only.
- Forgetting nil for the digit zero in a systematic name.
- Calling an anion smaller than its atom, or ordering isoelectronic ions by the radii of the parent atoms.
- Saying that ionisation enthalpy of oxygen exceeds that of nitrogen.
- Claiming fluorine has the most negative electron gain enthalpy.
- Giving a unit for electronegativity.
- Writing unbalanced equations for oxides.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Laws and definitions: one mark each, with the key phrase (atomic mass, atomic number, gaseous atoms, shared pair).
- Trend explanations: one mark for the trend, one for the reason (nuclear charge, shielding, size, subshell stability).
- Locating an element: one mark each for block, period and group.
- Equations: one mark for correct formulae, one for balancing.

cards.front_md: Why do we classify the elements?
cards.back_md: To study many elements through patterns and to predict the properties of new ones.

cards.front_md: Mendeleev’s periodic law?
cards.back_md: Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses.

cards.front_md: Two merits of Mendeleev’s table?
cards.back_md: It left gaps and predicted new elements (Ga, Ge, Sc); it corrected doubtful atomic masses.

cards.front_md: Name the element found as eka-silicon.
cards.back_md: Germanium (predicted mass 72, found 72.6).

cards.front_md: Three defects of Mendeleev’s table?
cards.back_md: Position of hydrogen; elements out of mass order (Ar, K); no place for isotopes.

cards.front_md: The modern periodic law?
cards.back_md: Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers (Moseley).

cards.front_md: Why do isotopes occupy one place in the modern table?
cards.back_md: They have the same atomic number.

cards.front_md: Number of periods and groups in the long form?
cards.back_md: 7 periods and 18 groups.

cards.front_md: Length of the periods?
Group number of a p-block element?
cards.back_md: 12 + number of electrons in the outer p subshell.

cards.front_md: Group number of a d-block element?
cards.back_md: Number of (n − 1)d plus ns electrons.

cards.front_md: Elements in the s, p, d and f blocks?
Name the metalloids.
cards.back_md: B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te.

cards.front_md: IUPAC numerical roots for 0 to 9?
cards.back_md: nil, un, bi, tri, quad, pent, hex, sept, oct, enn.

cards.front_md: Temporary name and symbol of Z = 114?
cards.back_md: Ununquadium, Uuq.

cards.front_md: Define atomic radius.
cards.back_md: Half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms: covalent (non-metals) or metallic (metals).

cards.front_md: Trend of atomic radius across a period and down a group?
cards.back_md: Decreases across a period; increases down a group.

cards.front_md: Why does the radius fall across a period?
cards.back_md: Nuclear charge rises, same shell, shielding about constant, so the effective nuclear charge grows.

cards.front_md: What is shielding?
cards.back_md: Reduction of the nuclear pull on an outer electron by the inner electrons.

cards.front_md: Cation versus atom, anion versus atom: size?
cards.back_md: A cation is smaller than its atom; an anion is larger.

cards.front_md: Order of radius for N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺?
cards.back_md: N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ (same electrons, rising Z).

cards.front_md: Define first ionisation enthalpy.
cards.back_md: Energy to remove the outermost electron from one mole of gaseous atoms (kJ mol⁻¹).

cards.front_md: Why is the ionisation enthalpy of N higher than that of O?
cards.back_md: N has a stable half-filled 2p³; in O the paired p electron is removed more easily.

cards.front_md: Why is B lower than Be in ionisation enthalpy?
cards.back_md: B’s outer electron is in a 2p orbital, higher in energy and shielded by 2s.

cards.front_md: Define electron gain enthalpy.
cards.back_md: Enthalpy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron; negative if energy is released.

cards.front_md: Which halogen has the most negative electron gain enthalpy?
cards.back_md: Chlorine (−349 kJ mol⁻¹), not fluorine (−328).

cards.front_md: Define electronegativity and its unit.
cards.back_md: Tendency of a bonded atom to attract the shared pair; no unit (Pauling scale, F = 4.0).

cards.front_md: Trend of metallic character?
cards.back_md: Decreases across a period; increases down a group.

cards.front_md: Valency toward oxygen of a main-group element?
cards.back_md: Equal to the group number (1 to 7).

cards.front_md: Why is NCl₅ unknown but PCl₅ known?
cards.back_md: Nitrogen has no d orbitals, so its covalence is limited to 4.

cards.front_md: Diagonal pairs?
cards.back_md: Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si.

cards.front_md: Nature of oxides across period 3?
cards.back_md: Strongly basic (Na₂O) → amphoteric (Al₂O₃) → strongly acidic (Cl₂O₇).

questions.stem_md: A chemist reading about Mendeleev’s work notes that gallium, discovered in 1875, matched his prediction for “eka-aluminium”, whose atomic mass he had given as about 68. The importance of this discovery was that it:

options.text_md: showed that the periodic law could predict the existence and properties of undiscovered elements
proved that elements must be arranged by atomic number and not by atomic mass
removed the difficulty of finding a place for the isotopes of an element
showed that every group of the table contains the same number of elements

questions.solution_md: The agreement between the predicted and observed properties of gallium gave strong support to the periodic law as a predictive tool — option (a). It did not show that atomic number is the true basis, which came later with Moseley.

questions.stem_md: Which defect of Mendeleev’s periodic table is removed when the elements are classified by atomic number?

options.text_md: Isotopes of one element, with different atomic masses, need not be given separate places
Elements of similar properties could not be placed in the same group
No gaps could be left for elements that were not yet discovered
The noble gases could not be accommodated in any group

questions.solution_md: Isotopes have the same atomic number, so they share one place in the modern table — option (a). The other three statements are not defects of Mendeleev’s table.

questions.stem_md: According to the modern periodic law, the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their:

options.text_md: atomic masses
mass numbers of the commonest isotopes
atomic numbers
number of neutrons in the nucleus

questions.solution_md: Moseley’s work led to the modern law: properties are a periodic function of atomic number — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In the modern periodic table cobalt (atomic mass 58.9) is placed before nickel (atomic mass 58.7).

**Reason (R):** In the modern periodic table the elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Cobalt (Z = 27) has a smaller atomic number than nickel (Z = 28), so it comes first although it has the larger mass. Both statements are true and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Because the modern periodic law uses atomic number, the isotopes of an element share a single position in the periodic table.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Isotopes have the same atomic number and so occupy one position.

questions.stem_md: Mendeleev predicted an atomic mass of $68$ for eka-aluminium. The element found, gallium, has atomic mass $69.7$. By what percentage of the true value is the prediction too low?
State two merits of Mendeleev’s periodic table and name one element whose discovery supported it.

answer.model_answer_md: Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties correctly, and he corrected doubtful atomic masses. The discovery of gallium (eka-aluminium), germanium (eka-silicon) or scandium (eka-boron) supported the table.

questions.solution_md: Gaps and predictions; corrected masses; gallium, germanium or scandium.

marking_scheme.step: One element named (Ga, Ge or Sc)

questions.stem_md: Give three defects of Mendeleev’s periodic table and say how the modern periodic law removes the one concerning the order of argon (39.9) and potassium (39.1).

answer.model_answer_md: Defects: (i) hydrogen has no fixed position; (ii) there was no separate place for isotopes; (iii) some elements, such as argon and potassium, had to be placed out of the order of atomic mass (also: dissimilar elements in the same group). Arranged by atomic number, argon (Z = 18) comes before potassium (Z = 19), so the order is correct although argon is heavier.

questions.solution_md: Three defects; atomic number order Ar (18), K (19).

marking_scheme.step: Ar (18) before K (19) by atomic number
Modern law uses atomic number, not atomic mass

questions.stem_md:
(a) State Mendeleev's periodic law and the modern periodic law. [2]

(b) Explain how Mendeleev's gaps and his prediction for eka-aluminium supported his law, naming the element that was found. [2]

(c) Give one reason why the modern periodic law is preferred. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Mendeleev: the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses. Modern law: the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.

(b) He left a gap below aluminium and predicted an element, eka-aluminium, with atomic mass about 68 and an oxide of formula Ea₂O₃; gallium, atomic mass 69.7 with oxide Ga₂O₃, was discovered and matched, showing that the law could predict unknown elements.

(c) Atomic number gives the correct order for pairs such as argon and potassium, and isotopes share one position.

questions.solution_md: Both laws; gallium matched eka-aluminium; atomic number removes anomalies.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Gap and predicted mass or oxide

questions.stem_md: An element has the valence configuration $4d^{10}\,5s^2\,5p^1$ with all inner shells complete. In the long form of the periodic table it belongs to:

options.text_md: the d block, period 5, group 12
the p block, period 4, group 13
the p block, period 5, group 3
the p block, period 5, group 13

questions.solution_md: The last electron enters a $5p$ orbital, so it is a p-block element; the highest shell is 5, so period 5; group $= 12 + 1 = 13$ — option (d). It is indium (Z = 49).

questions.stem_md: In the IUPAC numbering of the groups of the periodic table from 1 to 18, the halogens and the noble gases are in groups:

options.text_md: 17 and 18
7 and 8
16 and 17
17 and 0

questions.solution_md: Fluorine to astatine are in group 17 (old VIIA) and helium to radon in group 18 (old group 0) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Before a permanent name was approved, the element of atomic number 113 carried a temporary IUPAC name and symbol. These were:

options.text_md: unbitrium, Ubt
ununbium, Uub
ununtrium, Unt
ununtrium, Uut

questions.solution_md: The digits 1, 1, 3 give un, un, tri, so the name is ununtrium and the symbol is Uut (first letters U, u, t) — option (d). Option (a) is for Z = 123, option (b) for Z = 112, and in option (c) the symbol does not follow the order of the roots.

questions.stem_md: In the long form of the periodic table the fifth period begins with an alkali metal and ends with a noble gas. The number of elements in this period and the atomic number of the noble gas are, respectively:

options.text_md: 18 and 36
32 and 54
8 and 54
18 and 54

questions.solution_md: The fifth period fills $5s$, $4d$ and $5p$: $2 + 10 + 6 = 18$ elements, from Rb ($Z = 37$) to Xe ($Z = 36 + 18 = 54$) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A student looks up an element that lies in period 4 and group 15 of the long-form table. Its atomic number is:
questions.solution_md: Before period 4 there are 18 electrons ($[\text{Ar}]$); group 15 means $4s^2\,3d^{10}\,4p^3$, so $Z = 18 + 2 + 10 + 3 = 33$ (arsenic) — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Rubidium (Z = 37) is an element of period 5 and group 1.

**Reason (R):** The valence configuration of rubidium is 5s², with the 5s subshell completely filled.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the last electron enters 5s, so it is in period 5 and group 1. R is false: rubidium has the configuration [Kr] 5s¹, with a single electron in the 5s subshell — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The temporary IUPAC systematic name of the element of atomic number 118 is ___.
questions.solution_md: The digits 1, 1, 8 give un, un, oct, so the name is ununoctium.

questions.stem_md: Match each atomic number with the three-letter symbol of the temporary IUPAC name of that element.
questions.solution_md: 101 → s (Unu); 103 → q (Unt); 106 → p (Unh); 110 → r (Uun), built from the roots of the digits.

questions.stem_md: A steel alloy contains an element whose atoms have the outer configuration $3d^5\,4s^2$ outside an argon core. State its block, period and group in the long-form periodic table.

answer.model_answer_md: The last electron enters 3d, so the element is in the d block. The highest shell is n = 4, so it is in period 4; group = 5 + 2 = 7. (The element is manganese.)

questions.solution_md: d block, period 4, group 7.

questions.stem_md: Write the temporary IUPAC systematic name and the three-letter symbol of the element with atomic number 116, showing the root used for each digit.

answer.model_answer_md: The digits 1, 1, 6 correspond to un, un, hex, so the name is ununhexium and the symbol is Uuh.

questions.solution_md: ununhexium, Uuh.

questions.stem_md: Give the temporary IUPAC names and symbols for the elements with atomic numbers 109 and 125, and find the atomic number of the element whose systematic name is unnilhexium.

answer.model_answer_md: 109: un, nil, enn gives unnilennium, Une. 125: un, bi, pent gives unbipentium, Ubp. Unnilhexium: un, nil, hex gives the digits 1, 0, 6, so Z = 106.

questions.solution_md: unnilennium Une; unbipentium Ubp; Z = 106.

questions.stem_md: Write the electronic configurations of the elements of atomic numbers 31 and 40 and locate each in the long-form periodic table by block, period and group.

answer.model_answer_md: Z = 31: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p¹; last electron in 4p, so p block, period 4, group 13. Z = 40: [Kr] 4d² 5s²; last electron in 4d, so d block, period 5, group 4 (4 + ... valence electrons of 4d and 5s: 2 + 2 = 4).

marking_scheme.step: Configuration of Z = 31 and its position
Configuration of Z = 40 and its position

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the electronic configuration of the element of atomic number 34 and state its block, period and group. [2]

(b) An element has the configuration [Xe] 4f¹⁴ 5d¹⁰ 6s² 6p². Find its block, period and group. [2]

(c) Write the temporary IUPAC name and symbol of the element with Z = 111. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁴; last electron in 4p, so the p block, period 4, group 16 (12 + 4).

(b) The last electron enters 6p, so the p block; the highest shell is 6, so period 6; group = 12 + 2 = 14.

(c) 1, 1, 1 gives un, un, un: unununium, symbol Uuu.

questions.solution_md: Z = 34: p, 4, 16; Pb type: p, 6, 14; unununium Uuu.

questions.stem_md: Going from lithium (radius 152 pm) to fluorine (radius 64 pm) in the second period, the atomic radius falls because:

options.text_md: the number of shells increases, which draws the valence electrons closer to the nucleus
the nuclear charge falls as electrons are added, so the electrons repel one another less
the nuclear charge rises while the electrons enter the same shell, so shielding changes little and the valence electrons are pulled in more strongly
inner electrons shield the valence electrons more and more effectively

questions.solution_md: Across a period one proton and one valence electron are added in the same shell; electrons of the same shell shield one another poorly, so the effective nuclear charge rises and the radius falls — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The atomic radius of potassium (231 pm) is larger than that of sodium (186 pm) mainly because potassium:

options.text_md: has a smaller nuclear charge than sodium
has one more occupied shell, so the valence electron is farther from the nucleus and better shielded
has fewer valence electrons than sodium
has a smaller effective nuclear charge only because it has more neutrons

questions.solution_md: Down a group each period adds a shell: the valence electron is in a higher shell, farther away and more shielded, in spite of the larger nuclear charge — option (b). Both atoms have one valence electron, and neutrons play no part.

questions.stem_md: Among the species O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺, which has the largest radius?

options.text_md: F⁻
Na⁺
O²⁻
Mg²⁺

questions.solution_md: All four have 10 electrons, so the radius falls as the nuclear charge rises (8, 9, 11, 12). O²⁻ has the smallest nuclear charge and the largest radius (140 pm against 133, 102 and 72 pm) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Using the simple estimate that the effective nuclear charge $\approx Z -$ (number of inner-shell electrons), the effective nuclear charge felt by a valence electron of a phosphorus atom ($Z = 15$) is about:
questions.solution_md: Phosphorus has 10 inner electrons (1s, 2s, 2p), so $Z_\text{eff} \approx 15 - 10 = 5$ — option (a). 15 ignores shielding; 3 is the group-based valency; 8 is the sum of shell electrons.

questions.stem_md: How many valence electrons does an atom with the configuration $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10}\,4s^2\,4p^3$ have?
questions.solution_md: The valence shell is n = 4: 4s² 4p³ gives 2 + 3 = 5 electrons; the completed 3d subshell is part of the inner core for this p-block element — option (c). It is arsenic, in group 15.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The chloride ion (181 pm) is larger than the chlorine atom (99 pm).

**Reason (R):** The anion has one more electron than the atom, so electron–electron repulsion increases while the nuclear charge is unchanged.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the greater repulsion among 18 electrons held by the same nuclear charge (+17) expands the electron cloud, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Mg²⁺ ion (72 pm) is smaller than the Na⁺ ion (102 pm) because Mg²⁺ has more electrons than Na⁺.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Both ions have 10 electrons; Mg²⁺ is smaller because its nuclear charge (+12) is greater than that of Na⁺ (+11).

questions.stem_md: On going down a group of the periodic table the atomic radius generally ___.
questions.solution_md: Each period adds a shell, so the radius increases down a group.

questions.stem_md: In a crystal of iodine the distance between the nuclei of two bonded iodine atoms of a molecule is $266$ pm. Find the covalent radius of iodine in pm.
questions.solution_md: Covalent radius $= \dfrac{266}{2} = 133$ pm.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the shielding (screening) effect? How does it change down a group, and what is its effect on the atomic radius?

answer.model_answer_md: Shielding is the reduction of the attraction of the nucleus for an outer electron by the electrons in the inner shells. Down a group the number of inner shells increases, so the shielding increases, and together with the extra shell this makes the atomic radius larger.

questions.solution_md: Shielding by inner electrons; increases down the group; radius increases.

marking_scheme.step: Increases down a group, so radius rises

questions.stem_md: Explain why the sodium ion (102 pm) is much smaller than the sodium atom (186 pm).

answer.model_answer_md: In forming Na⁺ the atom loses its single 3s electron, so the outermost shell (n = 3) disappears and the ion has one shell fewer; the same nuclear charge (+11) now holds only 10 electrons, so each is pulled in more strongly and the repulsion is less.

questions.solution_md: Loss of the outer shell; greater pull per electron.

marking_scheme.step: Nuclear charge unchanged holds fewer electrons, less repulsion

questions.stem_md: The ions K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻ and S²⁻ (atomic numbers 19, 20, 17 and 16) are present in a mineral water sample. Arrange them in order of increasing radius and explain the order using their electrons and nuclear charges.

answer.model_answer_md: All four ions have 18 electrons (isoelectronic), so the radius depends only on the nuclear charge: the larger the charge, the stronger the pull on the same electron cloud. Nuclear charges are Ca 20, K 19, Cl 17, S 16, so the order of increasing radius is Ca²⁺ < K⁺ < Cl⁻ < S²⁻ (100, 138, 181, 184 pm).

questions.solution_md: Ca²⁺ < K⁺ < Cl⁻ < S²⁻

marking_scheme.step: Larger nuclear charge gives a smaller ion

questions.stem_md: Atomic radii in pm are Na 186, K 231, F 64 and Cl 99. Account for the difference between sodium and potassium and for the difference between fluorine and chlorine, and state the general trend they show.

answer.model_answer_md: Potassium (231 pm) is larger than sodium (186 pm), and chlorine (99 pm) is larger than fluorine (64 pm): in each pair the lower element has one more occupied shell, so the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded by the inner electrons. The general trend is that the atomic radius increases down a group.

questions.solution_md: Extra shell and more shielding; radius increases down a group.

marking_scheme.step: Na/K reason: extra shell, more shielding
F/Cl reason: extra shell, more shielding
General trend down a group stated

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain in terms of nuclear charge, shells and shielding why the atomic radius falls from lithium (152 pm) to fluorine (64 pm) across the second period. [3]

(b) The radius of the potassium atom is 231 pm and that of the K⁺ ion is 138 pm; the radius of the bromine atom is 114 pm and that of the Br⁻ ion is 195 pm. Explain both changes. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) From Li to F each atom has one more proton and one more electron, and the new electron enters the same shell (n = 2). Electrons in the same shell shield one another very little, so the shielding by the inner 1s electrons stays about the same while the nuclear charge increases from +3 to +9; the effective nuclear charge rises, the valence electrons are pulled closer and the radius decreases.

(b) K⁺ is smaller than K because the atom loses its 4s electron, so the outermost shell is gone and the nuclear charge (+19) now holds 18 electrons. Br⁻ is larger than Br because the added electron increases electron–electron repulsion while the nuclear charge (+35) is unchanged.

questions.solution_md: Rising Z, same shell, little extra shielding; cation loses a shell; anion has more repulsion.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Nuclear charge increases across the period
(a) Electrons enter the same shell, shielding about constant
(a) Effective nuclear charge rises so radius falls
(b) K⁺: outer shell lost, same charge holds fewer electrons

questions.stem_md: The first ionisation enthalpy of aluminium, 577 kJ mol⁻¹, is lower than that of magnesium, 737 kJ mol⁻¹, even though aluminium has the larger nuclear charge. The best explanation is that the outermost electron of aluminium:

options.text_md: is in a 3p orbital, which is higher in energy and better shielded by the 3s electrons than the 3s electron of magnesium
is in a 3s orbital that is shielded by the 3p electrons
is held by a smaller nuclear charge than the outer electron of magnesium
comes from a half-filled subshell that is unusually stable

questions.solution_md: Mg ([Ne] 3s²) loses a 3s electron; Al ([Ne] 3s² 3p¹) loses a 3p electron, which is farther out, higher in energy and shielded by the 3s electrons, so it is removed more easily — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A student explains that the first ionisation enthalpy of oxygen (1314 kJ mol⁻¹) is lower than that of nitrogen (1402 kJ mol⁻¹). The explanation is correct if she says that:

options.text_md: oxygen has a larger atomic radius than nitrogen by a large margin
in oxygen the fourth 2p electron shares an orbital and is repelled by its partner, whereas nitrogen has a stable half-filled 2p³ subshell
oxygen has a smaller nuclear charge than nitrogen
the 2p electrons of oxygen are shielded by a third shell

questions.solution_md: Nitrogen’s 2p³ is half filled and stable; in oxygen (2p⁴) one p orbital holds two electrons, whose repulsion makes one of them easier to remove — option (b). Oxygen’s radius is slightly smaller, its nuclear charge larger, and it has no third shell.

questions.stem_md: The first ionisation enthalpies of lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium and caesium are 520, 496, 419, 403 and 376 kJ mol⁻¹. The decrease down the group is mainly due to:

options.text_md: the decreasing nuclear charge down the group
the increasing size and shielding, which make the valence electron easier to remove
the increasing number of valence electrons
the increasing electronegativity of the atoms

questions.solution_md: Each element has one valence electron; down the group it lies in a higher shell, farther from the nucleus and shielded by more inner shells, so less energy is needed to remove it — option (b). The nuclear charge actually increases.

questions.stem_md: The electron gain enthalpies of F, Cl, Br and I are −328, −349, −325 and −295 kJ mol⁻¹. The largest amount of energy is released by the atom of:

options.text_md: fluorine, because it is the most electronegative and smallest atom
iodine, because it is the largest atom
bromine, because it has the greatest nuclear charge
chlorine, because the added electron meets less repulsion in its larger 3p shell than in the compact 2p shell of fluorine

questions.solution_md: Cl has the most negative value (−349). The F atom is so small that the added electron is strongly repelled by the electrons already in the 2p shell, so less energy is released than for Cl — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Using the Pauling electronegativities Na 0.9, Mg 1.2, Cl 3.0 and O 3.5, which of the bonds Na–Cl, Mg–O, Na–O and Mg–Cl has the greatest ionic character?

options.text_md: Na–Cl
Na–O
Mg–O
Mg–Cl

questions.solution_md: Differences in electronegativity: Na–Cl 2.1, Mg–O 2.3, Na–O 2.6, Mg–Cl 1.8. The largest difference, 2.6, is for Na–O — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which statement describes correctly the change in character of the group 14 elements C, Si, Ge, Sn and Pb down the group?

options.text_md: Metallic character decreases: lead is a non-metal and carbon is a metal
All five elements are non-metals with identical properties
Metallic character increases from carbon to silicon and then decreases to lead
Metallic character increases: carbon is a non-metal, silicon and germanium are metalloids, and tin and lead are metals

questions.solution_md: Ionisation enthalpy and electronegativity fall down a group, so metallic character rises: C non-metal, Si and Ge metalloids, Sn and Pb metals — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Sulfur has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than oxygen.

**Reason (R):** Elemental oxygen consists of diatomic molecules, whereas elemental sulfur consists of S₈ rings.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true (S −200, O −141 kJ mol⁻¹; O₂ molecules and S₈ rings), but R is not the explanation: electron gain enthalpy is a property of isolated gaseous atoms, not of how the element is bonded. The real reason is the strong repulsion an added electron meets in the small, compact 2p subshell of oxygen — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Neon has a large negative electron gain enthalpy.

**Reason (R):** The outer shell of neon is incomplete and readily accepts an additional electron.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are false. Neon has a positive electron gain enthalpy (+116 kJ mol⁻¹) because its outer shell is complete and an added electron would have to enter the next shell — option (d).

questions.stem_md: On the Pauling scale the most electronegative element, with a value of 4.0, is ___.
questions.solution_md: Fluorine is the most electronegative element (4.0).

questions.stem_md: A tube holds $2.4$ g of magnesium vapour (Mg $= 24$). Using the first ionisation enthalpy $737\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, calculate the energy needed to convert all the atoms into $\ce{Mg+}$ ions, in kJ.
The first three ionisation enthalpies of an element are 590, 1145 and 4912 kJ mol⁻¹ (calcium). How many valence electrons does it have?
questions.solution_md: Ratios: $1145/590 = 1.94$ and $4912/1145 = 4.29$. The big jump comes after the 2nd removal, so the number of valence electrons $= 2$ (group 2).

questions.stem_md: Define electronegativity. How does it change from sodium to chlorine across the third period, and why?

answer.model_answer_md: Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself. It increases from sodium (0.9) to chlorine (3.0) because the nuclear charge increases and the atomic radius decreases, so the attraction for the bonding electrons becomes stronger.

questions.solution_md: Definition; increases across, nuclear charge up and size down.

marking_scheme.step: Increases with reason (higher nuclear charge, smaller radius)

questions.stem_md: Define electron gain enthalpy and state why the noble gases have positive values.

answer.model_answer_md: The electron gain enthalpy is the enthalpy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron to form a gaseous anion. The noble gases have positive values because their outer shells are complete, so the added electron must go into a new, higher shell and energy has to be supplied.

questions.solution_md: Definition; complete shell, so the electron enters a higher shell.

questions.stem_md: Give the reason for each of the two reversals in the first ionisation enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹) of period 3: Mg 737 and Al 577; P 1012 and S 999.

answer.model_answer_md: Mg to Al: the outer electron of Al is in a 3p orbital, which is higher in energy and shielded by the 3s electrons, so it is removed more easily than the 3s electron of Mg although the nuclear charge is larger. P to S: phosphorus has a stable half-filled 3p³ subshell; in sulfur (3p⁴) two electrons share one orbital, and their repulsion makes one of them easier to remove, so S is lower than P.

questions.solution_md: Al: 3p above 3s; S: repulsion in the paired 3p orbital against half-filled P.

marking_scheme.step: P and S: half-filled 3p³ is stable
S: paired electrons repel and are easier to remove

questions.stem_md: The electron gain enthalpy of fluorine is −328 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of chlorine is −349 kJ mol⁻¹, although fluorine is the more electronegative. Explain this, and say whether the same happens for oxygen (−141) and sulfur (−200).

answer.model_answer_md: The fluorine atom is very small, and the electron it gains enters the compact 2p shell, which is already crowded with electrons, so the extra repulsion reduces the energy released. In chlorine the added electron enters the larger 3p subshell with less repulsion, so more energy is released. The same happens in group 16: sulfur (−200) is more negative than oxygen (−141).

questions.solution_md: Repulsion in the small 2p shell of F; Cl more negative; S more negative than O too.

marking_scheme.step: Compact 2p shell of fluorine, strong repulsion

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define the first ionisation enthalpy of an element and name two factors on which it depends. [2]

(b) The first ionisation enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹) are Be 899, B 801, N 1402, O 1314. Explain why B is lower than Be and O is lower than N. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The first ionisation enthalpy is the energy needed to remove the most loosely held electron from one mole of isolated gaseous atoms: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻. It depends on the nuclear charge, the atomic radius, the shielding by inner electrons, the type of orbital (penetration) and the stability of filled or half-filled subshells (any two).

(b) Be is 2s² and B is 2s² 2p¹: the 2p electron of boron is higher in energy and shielded by the 2s electrons, so it is removed more easily although the nuclear charge is larger. N is 2p³ (half filled and stable) and O is 2p⁴: in oxygen two electrons share one 2p orbital, and their repulsion makes one of them easier to remove, so O is lower than N.

questions.solution_md: Definition with two factors; p versus s electron; half-filled p³ versus paired p⁴.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Definition (gaseous atoms, outermost electron, per mole)
(b) B < Be: 2p higher in energy and shielded
(b) O: paired electrons repel, easier to remove

questions.stem_md: The oxide of a period 3 element is a white solid that dissolves in water to give an acidic solution and reacts with sodium hydroxide solution to form a salt. The element is most likely:

options.text_md: sodium, forming Na₂O
phosphorus, forming P₄O₁₀
magnesium, forming MgO
aluminium, forming Al₂O₃

questions.solution_md: P₄O₁₀ is an acidic oxide: it reacts with water to give phosphoric acid, $\ce{P4O10 + 6H2O -> 4H3PO4}$, and with alkalis to form phosphates — option (b). Na₂O and MgO are basic, and Al₂O₃ is amphoteric and insoluble in water.

questions.stem_md: The oxidation states of phosphorus in its common oxide P₄O₁₀ and in its hydride PH₃ are, respectively:

options.text_md: +5 and −3
+3 and −5
+5 and +3

questions.solution_md: In P₄O₁₀ each O is −2: 4x + 10(−2) = 0 gives x = +5. In PH₃ each H is +1: x + 3 = 0 gives x = −3 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a reason why lithium, beryllium and boron behave differently from the other members of their groups?

options.text_md: Their atoms have a larger radius than the elements below them
Their atoms have vacant d orbitals that allow expansion of the octet
Their atoms are small, with a high charge-to-size ratio and no d orbitals in the valence shell
Their atoms have the same electronegativity as the other group members

questions.solution_md: The second-period elements have small size, a high charge-to-size ratio and no d orbitals, so their covalence is limited to four and their polarising power is high — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Lithium resembles magnesium more closely than it resembles sodium. This is shown by lithium:

options.text_md: forming a superoxide when it burns in air
forming a nitride when it burns in nitrogen, as magnesium does
having a carbonate that is stable to heat
forming a stable solid hydrogencarbonate

questions.solution_md: Li and Mg both react directly with nitrogen: $\ce{6Li + N2 -> 2Li3N}$ and $\ce{3Mg + N2 -> Mg3N2}$ — option (b). Sodium does not form a nitride; Li₂CO₃ decomposes on heating, as MgCO₃ does.

questions.stem_md: Which pair of oxides shows amphoteric behaviour, reacting with both acids and strong bases?

options.text_md: MgO and Na₂O
SiO₂ and SO₃
CO₂ and P₄O₁₀
BeO and Al₂O₃

questions.solution_md: BeO and Al₂O₃ dissolve in acid and in alkali: $\ce{BeO + 2HCl -> BeCl2 + H2O}$ and $\ce{BeO + 2NaOH -> Na2BeO2 + H2O}$ — option (d). MgO and Na₂O are basic; SiO₂, SO₃, CO₂ and P₄O₁₀ are acidic.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Lithium and magnesium show a diagonal relationship.

**Reason (R):** Lithium and magnesium belong to the same period of the periodic table.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: Li and Mg resemble each other in several properties. R is false: Li is in period 2 and Mg in period 3; the pair lies on a diagonal, not in one period — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Nitrogen can form five covalent bonds, as in NCl₅, in the same way that phosphorus forms PCl₅.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Nitrogen has no d orbitals in its valence shell, so its covalence cannot exceed four and NCl₅ does not exist; phosphorus can use its 3d orbitals.

questions.stem_md: Match each period 3 element with the formula of its highest oxide.

options.text_md: Na
Mg
Al
P

questions.solution_md: Na → r (Na₂O); Mg → p (MgO); Al → s (Al₂O₃); P → q (P₄O₁₀).

questions.stem_md: In the oxide $\ce{Cl2O7}$ oxygen has oxidation state $-2$. Calculate the oxidation state of chlorine.
State two reasons why the first element of a group in the p-block, such as nitrogen, differs from the other members of its group.

answer.model_answer_md: Its atoms are small, with a high electronegativity and ionisation enthalpy (high charge-to-size ratio), and the valence shell has no d orbitals, so the maximum covalence is four. As a result N forms NCl₃ but not NCl₅, and it forms strong pπ–pπ multiple bonds such as N≡N.

questions.solution_md: Small size and high electronegativity; no d orbitals.

marking_scheme.step: Small size, high electronegativity or ionisation enthalpy
No d orbitals, covalence limited to four

questions.stem_md: State two properties in which lithium resembles magnesium but differs from sodium, and name this type of relationship.

answer.model_answer_md: Lithium and magnesium both form nitrides directly with nitrogen, and their carbonates decompose on heating to give the oxide and carbon dioxide (their hydroxides are also weakly basic). This is a diagonal relationship.

questions.solution_md: Nitrides; carbonates decompose; diagonal relationship.

questions.stem_md: Write balanced equations for (i) the reaction of $\ce{Na2O}$ with water, (ii) the reaction of $\ce{SO3}$ with water, and (iii) the reaction of $\ce{Al2O3}$ with sodium hydroxide, and state whether each oxide is basic, acidic or amphoteric.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) $\ce{Na2O + H2O -> 2NaOH}$: basic oxide. (ii) $\ce{SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4}$: acidic oxide. (iii) $\ce{Al2O3 + 2NaOH -> 2NaAlO2 + H2O}$: Al₂O₃ reacts with a base, and also with acids, so it is amphoteric.

questions.solution_md: Three balanced equations; basic, acidic, amphoteric.

questions.stem_md: Nitrogen forms NCl₃ only, whereas phosphorus forms both PCl₃ and PCl₅. Explain this difference using the valence shells of the two atoms.

answer.model_answer_md: Both atoms have five valence electrons and can form three bonds to give NCl₃ and PCl₃. A nitrogen atom has only the 2s and 2p orbitals in its valence shell, no d orbitals, so it cannot hold more than four pairs and cannot form five bonds; NCl₅ does not exist. A phosphorus atom has vacant 3d orbitals, so it can promote an electron and expand its octet to form five bonds in PCl₅.

questions.solution_md: Both form MCl₃; N has no d orbitals; P has vacant 3d orbitals.

marking_scheme.step: Both form three bonds, five valence electrons
N: no d orbitals, covalence at most four

questions.stem_md: Explain what is meant by a diagonal relationship. Give two similarities between lithium and magnesium, with the equation for one of the reactions.

answer.model_answer_md: A diagonal relationship is the similarity between an element of the second period and the element diagonally below and to the right of it in the third period, such as Li and Mg; the pairs have similar electronegativity and charge-to-size ratio. Li and Mg both form nitrides directly, $\ce{6Li + N2 -> 2Li3N}$ and $\ce{3Mg + N2 -> Mg3N2}$, and their carbonates decompose on heating.

questions.solution_md: Definition; nitride formation with an equation; carbonate decomposition.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is a diagonal relationship? Give the reason why diagonal pairs resemble one another. [2]

(b) Give two similarities between beryllium and aluminium, and write balanced equations to show that beryllium oxide is amphoteric. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) It is the similarity in properties between an element of period 2 and the element one place to the right in the next period, such as Li–Mg, Be–Al and B–Si. Moving across a period the size decreases and electronegativity rises, and moving down a group the opposite happens, so the charge-to-size ratio and electronegativity of the diagonal pair are nearly equal (Be and Al are both 1.5).

(b) Both Be and Al have amphoteric oxides, and both form covalent chlorides (BeCl₂ and AlCl₃) that are soluble in organic solvents. BeO reacts with an acid, showing basic behaviour: $\ce{BeO + 2HCl -> BeCl2 + H2O}$; it also reacts with an alkali, showing acidic behaviour: $\ce{BeO + 2NaOH -> Na2BeO2 + H2O}$.

questions.solution_md: Definition and reason; two similarities; two equations.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Reason: similar charge-to-size ratio and electronegativity

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe how the nature of the oxides changes across period 3 from Na₂O to Cl₂O₇, giving the nature of each of Na₂O, Al₂O₃, SiO₂ and SO₃. [3]

(b) Write balanced equations to show that Al₂O₃ is amphoteric. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The oxides change from strongly basic through amphoteric to strongly acidic, as the electronegativity of the element rises and the bond to oxygen changes from ionic to covalent. Na₂O is strongly basic, Al₂O₃ is amphoteric, SiO₂ is weakly acidic and SO₃ is strongly acidic (Cl₂O₇ is very strongly acidic).

(b) With acid: $\ce{Al2O3 + 6HCl -> 2AlCl3 + 3H2O}$; with alkali: $\ce{Al2O3 + 2NaOH -> 2NaAlO2 + H2O}$.

questions.solution_md: Basic to amphoteric to acidic; two balanced equations for Al₂O₃.
